answer_text:
Let \(A\in \mathbb{C}^{n\times n}\) (the real case is the same, using complex eigenvalues). Put \(A\) in Jordan form

\[
A=VJV^{-1},\qquad J=\bigoplus J_{m_i}(\lambda_i),
\]

so that

\[
e^{At}=V e^{Jt}V^{-1}.
\]

For one Jordan block \(J_m(\lambda)=\lambda I+N\), with \(N^m=0\),

\[
e^{tJ_m(\lambda)}
= e^{\lambda t}\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}\frac{t^r}{r!}N^r.
\]

Hence:

- If \(\Re \lambda<0\), then \(e^{tJ_m(\lambda)}\to 0\).
- If \(\Re \lambda>0\), the block is unbounded, so no finite limit.
- If \(\Re \lambda=0\) and \(\lambda\neq 0\), then \(e^{\lambda t}=e^{i\omega t}\) oscillates, so no limit.
- If \(\lambda=0\), then \(e^{tJ_m(0)}=I+tN+\cdots\); this converges iff \(m=1\), i.e. \(0\) is semisimple, in which case the limit is \(I\).

Therefore the finite limit exists exactly when every nonzero eigenvalue of \(A\) has negative real part, and the eigenvalue \(0\), if present, is semisimple. In that case the limit is the spectral projector onto the zero eigenspace \(\ker A\).

\[
\boxed{
\lim_{t\to\infty}e^{At}=
\begin{cases}
P_0, & \text{if } \Re\lambda<0 \text{ for all } \lambda\in\sigma(A)\setminus\{0\}, \\
& \text{and } 0\notin\sigma(A)\text{ or }0\text{ is semisimple},\\[1mm]
\text{does not exist as a finite matrix}, & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
}
\]

Here \(P_0\) is the projector onto \(\ker A\); if \(A=VJV^{-1}\) has \(k\) zero eigenvalues, all in \(1\times1\) Jordan blocks, then

\[
P_0=V\operatorname{diag}(0,\ldots,0,1,\ldots,1)V^{-1},
\]

with \(P_0=0\) if \(0\notin\sigma(A)\).

27B·v4.method: Jordan canonical form decomposes e^{At} into blocks; each block's limit is determined by eigenvalue real part and block size; result assembles to a spectral projector P₀.
